recall_prompt: Say how you would solve this reciprocal equation — what you divide by, what you substitute, and how each value of t gives two roots.
insider_note: Every root here is rational, so both endings factorise; a surd in the answer means a slip in the t values.

steps.label: Reciprocal form
steps.margin_note: First mark. Coefficients 6, −35, 62, −35, 6 read the same both ways and the degree is even. Divide by x² and pair 6x² with 6/x², 35x with 35/x.
steps.memory_tip: 6, −35, 62, −35, 6 reads the same both ways, degree even. Divide by x² and pair the ends.
lines: Degree n = 4 is even, and aₖ = aₙ₋ₖ for every k
So this is a standard reciprocal equation.
x ≠ 0, so divide every term by x²:

recall.must_convey: That the degree is even and the coefficients 6, −35, 62, −35, 6 read the same from both ends, so the equation is a standard reciprocal equation, and that dividing by x² lets the terms be grouped in pairs.
accept: the degree is even and the coefficients are the same from both ends so it is a standard reciprocal equation, divide by x square and group the terms
coefficients read the same forwards and backwards so divide through by x squared and pair x squared with one by x squared
identify it as a reciprocal equation and divide by x square
coefficients rendu vaipula same, kabatti reciprocal equation, x square tho divide chesi group cheyyali
it is reciprocal because a k equals a n minus k, so divide every term by x squared
heard_as: a k equals a n minus k

steps.why: A standard reciprocal equation of even degree 2m can always be cut to a degree-m equation in t = x + 1/x, because dividing by xᵐ pairs each term with its matching term from the other end. Checking the symmetry first is what earns the right to that shortcut.
common_mistakes: Dividing by x² but writing the terms in the wrong pairs (x² must pair with 1/x², x with 1/x).
Calling every symmetric-looking equation reciprocal without checking every coefficient pair.
Forgetting to note x ≠ 0 before dividing (0 is not a root, since the constant term is not 0).

steps.label: Put x + 1/x = t
lines: Put x + 1/x = t, so x² + 1/x² = t² − 2

recall.must_convey: That x + 1/x is replaced by t, and that x² + 1/x² is then t² − 2 (from squaring), which turns the equation into a quadratic in t.
accept: put x plus one by x equal to t so x squared plus one by x squared is t squared minus two and the equation becomes a quadratic in t
substitute t for x plus one over x and use t squared minus two for the squared pair
let x plus one by x be t, square it, and the pair of squares is t square minus two
x plus one by x ni t ga pettali, x square plus one by x square ante t square minus two
the substitution is t equals x plus its reciprocal, and the squared pair is t squared minus two

steps.why: x² + 1/x² is NOT t²; squaring t = x + 1/x gives t² = x² + 2 + 1/x², so the pair of squares is t² − 2. This one identity is the whole method — every mark after it depends on the −2 being there.
common_mistakes: Writing x² + 1/x² = t² and losing the −2.
Substituting for x + 1/x but leaving x² + 1/x² unchanged.

steps.label: Solve for t
steps.margin_note: Third mark. Split the middle term: −35 = −20 − 15 with (−20)(−15) = 300 = 6 × 50.

recall.must_convey: That the quadratic in t is factorised (or solved) to give the two values of t.
accept: factorise the quadratic in t and get the two values of t
solve the t equation by splitting the middle term
the quadratic in t factors and gives two t values
t quadratic ni factorise chesi rendu t values teeskovali
split the middle term of the t equation and read off t

steps.why: The t-equation is a plain quadratic, so factorising it is the cheapest way to the two values of t. Each t value will give two x values, so the count of roots (2 × 2 = 4) is checked here before any x is found.
common_mistakes: A sign slip when splitting the middle term.
Stopping at the two t values as if they were the roots.
Solving the t-quadratic with the formula and making an arithmetic slip a factorisation would have avoided.

steps.label: t = 10/3
steps.margin_note: Two marks. Multiply x + 1/x = 10/3 by 3x: 3x² − 10x + 3 = 0, which factorises as (3x − 1)(x − 3). 10/3 = 3 + 1/3 reads the same roots off directly.
steps.memory_tip: Multiply by 3x: 3x² − 10x + 3 = (3x − 1)(x − 3). Also 10/3 = 3 + 1/3 reads the roots off directly.

recall.must_convey: That t = 10/3 is put back into x + 1/x = t, multiplied out to a quadratic in x, and solved to give the roots 3 and 1/3.
accept: put t equals 10/3 back so x plus one by x is 10/3 multiply by x to get a quadratic and solve it
x plus one over x equals 10/3 gives a quadratic in x whose roots are 3 and 1/3
go back from t equals 10/3 to a quadratic in x and solve
t equals 10/3 ni tirigi x plus one by x lo petti quadratic solve cheyyali
multiply x plus one by x equals 10/3 through by x and use the quadratic formula

steps.why: Each value of t gives two values of x, because x + 1/x = t is a quadratic in x. Solving both t values is what recovers all 4 roots of the original equation — stopping at t answers a different question.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to multiply through by x, so the equation in x is never formed.
Using the quadratic formula on 3x² − 10x + 3 and making an arithmetic slip that the factorisation (3x − 1)(x − 3) would have avoided.
Writing down only one root of the pair: (3x − 1)(x − 3) = 0 gives both x = 3 and x = 1/3.

steps.label: t = 5/2
steps.margin_note: Last two marks. 2x² − 5x + 2 = 0 factorises as (2x − 1)(x − 2). All four roots are rational here; box them together. Their product is 3 · (1/3) · 2 · (1/2) = 1 = 6/6.
steps.memory_tip: 2x² − 5x + 2 = (2x − 1)(x − 2). Every root here is rational — a surd means a slip in t.

recall.must_convey: That t = 5/2 is put back into x + 1/x = t, multiplied out to a quadratic in x, and solved to give the roots 2 and 1/2.
accept: put t equals 5/2 back so x plus one by x is 5/2 multiply by x to get a quadratic and solve it
x plus one over x equals 5/2 gives a quadratic in x whose roots are 2 and 1/2
go back from t equals 5/2 to a quadratic in x and solve
t equals 5/2 ni tirigi x plus one by x lo petti quadratic solve cheyyali
multiply x plus one by x equals 5/2 through by x and use the quadratic formula

steps.why: Each value of t gives two values of x, because x + 1/x = t is a quadratic in x. Solving both t values is what recovers all 4 roots of the original equation — stopping at t answers a different question.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to multiply through by x, so the equation in x is never formed.
Using the quadratic formula on 2x² − 5x + 2 and making an arithmetic slip that the factorisation (2x − 1)(x − 2) would have avoided.
Writing down only one root of the pair: (2x − 1)(x − 2) = 0 gives both x = 2 and x = 1/2.
